answer:
**The meta-analysis (Lancet 2014, PMID 24315724)** pooled all 71,683 participants from RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (42,411 on a new oral anticoagulant, 29,272 on warfarin). It concluded that, versus warfarin, new oral anticoagulants:

- reduced stroke or systemic embolic events by 19% (RR 0·81, 95% CI 0·73–0·91; p<0·0001), mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (0·49, 0·38–0·64; p<0·0001);
- reduced all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85–0·95; p=0·0003);
- reduced intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39–0·59; p<0·0001);
- but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (1·25, 1·01–1·55; p=0·04).

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"New oral anticoagulants significantly reduced stroke or systemic embolic events by 19% compared with warfarin (RR 0·81, 95% CI 0·73-0·91; p<0·0001), mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (0·49, 0·38-0·64; p<0·0001). New oral anticoagulants also significantly reduced all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85-0·95; p=0·0003) and intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39-0·59; p<0·0001), but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (1·25, 1·01-1·55; p=0·04)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"We did a prespecified meta-analysis of all 71,683 participants included in the RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 trials."} -->

**ELDERCARE-AF (Low-Dose Edoxaban in Very Elderly Patients with Atrial Fibrillation):** In 984 elderly Japanese patients (≥80 years) with nonvalvular AF who were not appropriate candidates for standard-dose anticoagulation, randomized 1:1 to 15 mg edoxaban once daily (492) or placebo (492), the annualized rate of stroke or systemic embolism was 2.3% with edoxaban versus 6.7% with placebo (HR 0.34; 95% CI 0.19–0.61; P<0.001), and major bleeding was 3.3% versus 1.8% (HR 1.87; 95% CI 0.90–3.89; P=0.09). - No substantial between-group difference in all-cause death (9.9% edoxaban vs 10.2% placebo; HR 0.97; 95% CI 0.69–1.36).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_0e9d75e95b4aa172897de8e3f4333228","quote":"There was no substantial between-group difference in death from any cause (9.9% in the edoxaban group and 10.2% in the placebo group; hazard ratio, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.69 to 1.36)."} -->

Note on comparability: ENGAGE and the meta-analysis compare low-dose edoxaban against warfarin, whereas ELDERCARE-AF compares 15 mg edoxaban against placebo in patients deemed unsuitable for standard-dose anticoagulation — so the numbers are not directly comparable across the three.

The same document also reports that the primary outcome occurred at 1.27% per year with apixaban vs. 1.60% per year with warfarin (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.66–0.95), and death from any cause at 3.52% vs. 3.94% (HR 0.89; 95% CI 0.80–0.99).

answer:
In AVERROES (apixaban vs aspirin in 5,599 patients with atrial fibrillation at increased stroke risk for whom vitamin K antagonist therapy was unsuitable, mean follow-up 1.1 years), the hazard ratio for the primary outcome of stroke or systemic embolism with apixaban was **0.45 (95% CI, 0.32 to 0.62; P<0.001)** — 51 events (1.6% per year) with apixaban versus 113 (3.7% per year) with aspirin. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"There were 51 primary outcome events (1.6% per year) among patients assigned to apixaban and 113 (3.7% per year) among those assigned to aspirin (hazard ratio with apixaban, 0.45; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.32 to 0.62; P<0.001)."} -->

The trial was terminated early on the recommendation of the data and safety monitoring board, because of a clear benefit in favor of apixaban. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"The data and safety monitoring board recommended early termination of the study because of a clear benefit in favor of apixaban."} -->

For context, death rates were 3.5% vs 4.4% per year (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.62–1.02; P=0.07) and major bleeding 44 vs 39 cases (HR 1.13; 95% CI 0.74–1.75; P=0.57). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_ee77d1914d18a5ece9857b4e40a81405","quote":"The rates of death were 3.5% per year in the apixaban group and 4.4% per year in the aspirin group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.62 to 1.02; P=0.07)."} -->

answer:
**Primary composite outcome (CV death or HF hospitalization):**

- **DAPA-HF** (HFrEF): HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65–0.85; P<0.001) — 16.3% vs 21.2% over a median 18.2 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 patients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85; P<0.001)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Reduced**: HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.65–0.86; P<0.001) — 19.4% vs 24.7% over a median 16 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 361 of 1863 patients (19.4%) in the empagliflozin group and in 462 of 1867 patients (24.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.86; P<0.001)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Preserved** (EF >40%): HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.69–0.90; P<0.001) — 13.8% vs 17.1% over a median 26.2 months, driven mainly by fewer HF hospitalizations.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)"} -->
- **DELIVER** (EF >40%): HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.73–0.92; P<0.001) — 16.4% vs 19.5% over a median 2.3 years; worsening HF HR 0.79, CV death HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05, not significant).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)"} -->

**Across the ejection fraction range:** the benefit is consistent. In the meta-analysis of the two mildly reduced/preserved-EF trials (12,251 participants), the composite was reduced with HR 0.80 (0.73–0.87), with consistent reductions in both components (CV death 0.88, 0.77–1.00; first HF hospitalization 0.74, 0.67–0.83).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Among 12 251 participants from DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0·80 [95% CI 0·73-0·87]) with consistent reductions in both components"} -->
Across all five trials (21,947 participants), the composite fell to 0.77 (0.72–0.82), with treatment effects generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction."} -->

So the relative reduction is somewhat smaller at higher ejection fractions (0.74–0.75 in HFrEF vs 0.79–0.82 in mildly reduced/preserved EF), but the effect is statistically significant and directionally consistent at every point of the EF spectrum.

- **ASCEND** (15,480 adults with diabetes, no evident cardiovascular disease): serious vascular events significantly lower with aspirin — 658 (8.5%) vs 743 (9.6%); rate ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.79–0.97; P=0.01, over a mean 7.4 years. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"During a mean follow-up of 7.4 years, serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01)."} --> But major bleeding rose (314 [4.1%] vs 245 [3.2%]; rate ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.09–1.52; P=0.003), so the absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"Aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) occurred in 61 (0·97%) patients in the aspirin group versus 29 (0·46%) in the placebo group (HR 2·11; 95% CI 1·36-3·28; p=0·0007)."} -->

answer:
**ASPREE** (Effect of Aspirin on All-Cause Mortality in the Healthy Elderly): among 19,114 community-dwelling adults ≥70 years (≥65 for US blacks and Hispanics) without cardiovascular disease, dementia or disability, randomized to 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo, all-cause mortality was higher with aspirin — 12.7 vs 11.1 events per 1000 person-years (HR 1.14; 95% CI 1.01–1.29), over a median 4.7 years and 1052 deaths.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29)."} -->
The excess was attributed primarily to cancer-related death: cancer accounted for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years, with cancer death in 3.1% on aspirin vs 2.3% on placebo (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.10–1.56).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"Cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years."} -->
The authors called this result unexpected and said it should be interpreted with caution.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_400696c0380783b1753ade39d010ccba","quote":"In the context of previous studies, this result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution."} -->

**ARRIVE** (Use of aspirin to reduce risk of initial vascular events): in 12,546 moderate-CVD-risk patients, median 60 months, there were 321 deaths in the intention-to-treat population — 160 (2.55%) with aspirin vs 161 (2.57%) with placebo, i.e. no mortality difference.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"There were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (n=160 [2·55%] vs n=161 [2·57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group)."} -->

answer:
## The three trials

**ARRIVE** (Lancet 2018) enrolled patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event: eligible patients were aged 55 years or older for men and 60 years or older for women, with average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded. 12,546 patients were enrolled at 501 sites between July 2007 and November 2016, with median follow-up of 60 months; the primary endpoint occurred in 4.29% on aspirin vs 4.48% on placebo (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)."} -->

**ASPREE** (NEJM 2018) enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) who did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, from 2010 through 2014; participants received 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo. Low-dose aspirin resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and no significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} -->

**JPPP** (JAMA 2014) was a multicenter, open-label, randomized trial of 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up for up to 6.5 years (last follow-up May 2012).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

## USPSTF recommendation (2022 statement)

Population: adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be individual; net benefit is small, with moderate certainty, and those not at increased bleeding risk willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit (C recommendation).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->
- **Ages 60 or older:** the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin in this group has no net benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

## How they relate

The recommendation is built on a systematic review of aspirin for primary prevention in persons without a history of CVD, including effects on colorectal cancer incidence/mortality and harms (particularly bleeding), plus a commissioned microsimulation model stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF also commissioned a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms from aspirin use for primary prevention of CVD and CRC, stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level."} -->

- ASPREE and JPPP fall squarely in the age group for which the USPSTF recommends against initiation — ASPREE enrolled adults ≥70 (≥65 for blacks and Hispanics), JPPP adults 60–85 — and their findings of increased major hemorrhage without a significant cardiovascular benefit in older adults align with the "no net benefit" conclusion at ≥60 years.
- ARRIVE's population (men ≥55, women ≥60, moderate risk, diabetes and high bleeding risk excluded) sits at the boundary of the two age bands: the trial's null efficacy result (HR 0.96) supports the small-net-benefit, individual-decision framing for 40–59-year-olds, but the trial's own age criteria extend into the ≥60 group, where the recommendation is against initiation. Note that ARRIVE excluded diabetes, whereas JPPP required at least one of hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes — so the trial populations differ from each other and from the broader recommended population, which includes patients not at increased bleeding risk.

## The three trials

**ARRIVE** (Lancet 2018) enrolled patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event: eligible patients were aged 55 years or older for men and 60 years or older for women, with average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded. 12,546 patients were enrolled at 501 sites between July 2007 and November 2016, with median follow-up of 60 months; the primary endpoint occurred in 4.29% on aspirin vs 4.48% on placebo (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)."} -->

**ASPREE** (NEJM 2018) enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) who did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, from 2010 through 2014; participants received 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo. Low-dose aspirin resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and no significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} -->

**JPPP** (JAMA 2014) was a multicenter, open-label, randomized trial of 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up for up to 6.5 years (last follow-up May 2012).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

## USPSTF recommendation (2022 statement)

Population: adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be individual; net benefit is small, with moderate certainty, and those not at increased bleeding risk willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit (C recommendation).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->
- **Ages 60 or older:** the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin in this group has no net benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

## How they relate

The recommendation is built on a systematic review of aspirin for primary prevention in persons without a history of CVD, including effects on colorectal cancer incidence/mortality and harms (particularly bleeding), plus a commissioned microsimulation model stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF also commissioned a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms from aspirin use for primary prevention of CVD and CRC, stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level."} -->

- ASPREE and JPPP fall squarely in the age group for which the USPSTF recommends against initiation — ASPREE enrolled adults ≥70 (≥65 for blacks and Hispanics), JPPP adults 60–85 — and their findings of increased major hemorrhage without a significant cardiovascular benefit in older adults align with the "no net benefit" conclusion at ≥60 years.
- ARRIVE's population (men ≥55, women ≥60, moderate risk, diabetes and high bleeding risk excluded) sits at the boundary of the two age bands: the trial's null efficacy result (HR 0.96) supports the small-net-benefit, individual-decision framing for 40–59-year-olds, but the trial's own age criteria extend into the ≥60 group, where the recommendation is against initiation. Note that ARRIVE excluded diabetes, whereas JPPP required at least one of hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes — so the trial populations differ from each other and from the broader recommended population, which includes patients not at increased bleeding risk.
